title: What "8000W" Really Means on a Blender in Ghana
excerpt: Almost every blender sold in Ghana claims 4500W or 8000W. On a Ghanaian socket, both numbers are physically impossible. Here is the arithmetic, and the real number.
content:
Quick answer. No blender plugged into a Ghanaian wall socket can draw 8000W, or 4500W. A Type G socket delivers at most 2,990W and a Type D at most 1,380W. The number on the box is a peak marketing figure. Real continuous draw on a typical 2L commercial blender is around 600W, which costs about GHS 6.11 a month to run.

The arithmetic anyone can check

Ghana's mains supply is 230 volts. Power is volts multiplied by amps. The two domestic socket types set a hard ceiling:

SocketRated ampsMaximum deliverable power
Type G (the rectangular three pin)13A230 x 13 = 2,990W
Type D (the round three pin)6A230 x 6 = 1,380W

An 8000W load would need 34.8 amps, which is 2.7 times what a Type G socket can supply and 5.8 times a Type D. The fuse in the plug blows long before the motor ever sees that power. A 4500W claim needs 19.6 amps and fails the same test.

So why is the number on the box?

It is a peak or stall figure: the instantaneous surge at motor startup, or the theoretical maximum the windings could momentarily survive. It is not what the motor draws while blending your pepper. The same trick inflates horsepower claims on premium blender brands worldwide. One horsepower is 746 watts, so treat these labels as marketing units rather than electrical ones.

What it actually costs you to run

At the PURC residential rate of GHS 2.04 per kWh, effective 1 July 2026, ten minutes of blending a day comes to:

Real continuous drawkWh per monthCost per month
300W1.5GHS 3.06
600W (typical 2L commercial)3.0GHS 6.11
800W4.0GHS 8.15
1200W6.0GHS 12.23

Here is the part that should change how you shop: the blender, the appliance with the scariest number on the box, is one of the cheapest things in your kitchen to run. The quiet ones are the expensive ones. A double burner hot plate at typical use costs about GHS 91.69 a month.

What to look at instead of the wattage

Jar size for your family, whether it comes with a genuine dry mill if you grind grains and spices, blade metal, and whether the seller holds local stock so a warranty claim has somewhere to go. Every blender we sell states its realistic draw class, its running cost at the current tariff, and its price verified for the current month.

Sources and working: PURC Q2 2026 tariff decision plus the 3.49 per cent increase effective 1 July 2026; Ghana mains 230V; socket ratings per the Type G (13A) and Type D (6A) standards. Cost formula: watts / 1000 x hours per day x 30 x rate.

title: What 30,000mAh Really Delivers to Your Phone
excerpt: A power bank never delivers its advertised mAh. The physics is settled and the arithmetic is simple. Here is the real number, and how many charges you actually get.
content:
Quick answer. A "30,000mAh" power bank delivers roughly 15,500 to 18,900mAh to your phone, about three to four full charges of a typical 5,000mAh battery, not six. This is true of every brand at every price. The cells store charge at 3.7 volts, your phone receives it at 5 volts, and the conversion between them loses energy as heat.

The formula

Energy is conserved in watt hours, not milliamp hours. The advertised mAh is measured at the cell voltage, and delivery happens at USB voltage:

Real mAh at 5V = (3.7 x advertised mAh x efficiency) / 5.0

Quality units convert at about 85 per cent efficiency. Budget units, which is most of what sells in Accra, run nearer 70 per cent.

AdvertisedStored energyReal at 5V (budget)Real at 5V (quality)
10,000mAh37.0 Wh5,180mAh6,290mAh
20,000mAh74.0 Wh10,360mAh12,580mAh
30,000mAh111.0 Wh15,540mAh18,870mAh

The industry already admits this

Anker publishes the same arithmetic for its own products, quoting roughly 82 per cent efficiency and a "rated capacity" near 6,068mAh on a 10,000mAh bank. The information is not hidden. It is just never said at the point of sale in Ghana.

How many charges you actually get

Divide the real delivered figure by your phone's battery. A 5,000mAh phone gets about one full charge from a 10,000mAh bank, two from a 20,000mAh, and three to four from a 30,000mAh. If a listing promises six charges from 30,000mAh, the seller has not done the arithmetic, or hopes you will not.

One more thing before you fly

Airlines generally cap carry-on batteries at 100Wh without approval. A 30,000mAh unit stores about 111Wh, over that line. Up to 20,000mAh (74Wh) travels without questions.

Why we tell you this

Because you already know your power bank underdelivers. You have owned one. We would rather be the shop that explains why, with the working on the page, than the fifth listing shouting a number physics does not permit. Every power bank we sell states its honest charge count, and its price is verified for the current month.

title: Why A GHS 280 Blender Grinds Pepper Better Than A GHS 900 One
excerpt: The expensive blender on the shelf is built for smoothies. Ghanaian pepper needs the opposite thing. Here is the mechanism, and what it means for what you should buy.
content:
Quick answer. Grinding pepper needs turning force at low speed, not blade speed. Cheap Ghanaian-market blenders use high-torque motors with narrow, steep jars, which is exactly right for pepper, ginger and groundnut. Expensive smoothie blenders optimise for speed in a wide jar, which whips soft fruit beautifully and stalls on a dry chilli. This is why a GHS 280 machine out-grinds a GHS 900 one on the job you actually do.

The moment this matters

It is six in the morning. You have half a bowl of dried pepper, ginger, garlic and a little onion, and you want it ground before the children wake. You switch on, the motor screams, and the pepper sits at the top of the jar spinning around the blade without ever meeting it. You add water you did not want to add. That is not a bad blender. That is a blender built for a different job.

Torque and speed are not the same thing

Every motor trades one for the other. Speed is how fast the blade spins. Torque is how hard it keeps spinning when something resists it.

Soft fruit offers almost no resistance, so a smoothie machine can chase speed. Dried pepper, ginger and groundnut are hard and dry. They resist. The moment a high-speed low-torque blade meets them it slows, and a slowing blade cannot cut. You hear it as the motor note dropping, then you hear it rise again as the blade spins free in a pocket of air it has carved for itself.

A high-torque motor does the opposite. It turns slower and refuses to be stopped. It keeps chewing.

The jar matters as much as the motor

This is the part almost nobody is told. A smoothie jar is wide at the base so liquid can circulate. A grinding jar is narrow and steep, so gravity keeps feeding dry material back down onto the blade instead of letting it climb the walls.

Look at the two jars side by side on the shelf. The one that looks cheap and narrow is the one that will grind your pepper dry, without added water, which is what you want if you are making shito or storing a batch.

The number to look at instead of wattage

The wattage printed on the box is a peak marketing figure. We have covered why in a separate piece: a Ghanaian 13A socket can deliver at most 2,990W, so any blender claiming 4500W or 8000W is quoting something that cannot physically happen in your kitchen.

What to look at instead:

  • Jar shape. Narrow and steep for dry grinding. Wide for drinks.
  • A separate dry mill. The small cup with the flat blade. If it has one, it is built with grinding in mind.
  • The coupling. The part joining motor to jar. Metal outlasts plastic by years on a machine used daily.
  • Weight. A heavier base usually means more copper in the motor, which usually means more torque.

What we found on the ground

In July 2026 we priced 2L commercial-style blenders with a dry mill across Accra dealers. The working range was GHS 280 to GHS 340. The same shelves carried imported smoothie machines from GHS 850 upward that grind soft fruit better and dry pepper worse.

If your kitchen mostly makes pepper, shito, ginger and groundnut, the cheaper machine is not a compromise. It is the correct tool, and you keep the difference.

Who should buy which

Buy the commercial-style grinder if you cook Ghanaian food daily, make shito in batches, or sell food. It will grind dry, and the metal coupling survives daily use.

Buy the smoothie machine if you mainly make drinks, smoothies and soups, and grind pepper only occasionally with a little water.

Check it before you pay

When the rider reaches you, before any money changes hands: lift the base and feel the weight, turn the jar to check the coupling is metal and seats firmly, and run it empty for five seconds to hear whether the motor note is steady. If anything is not as described, do not pay. That is the whole point of pay on delivery.

See the blenders we stock, each with the real jar type and coupling material stated. Pay on delivery in Accra, same day where we can.

title: How Long A Rechargeable Fan Really Runs When The Light Goes
excerpt: Two fans claim the same battery and one dies at 2am while the other is still turning at dawn. The difference is the motor, not the battery. Here are the real hours.
content:
Quick answer. Two rechargeable fans with the same advertised battery can differ by three times in real runtime, because runtime is set by how much current the motor draws, not by the battery alone. A brushless motor on speed one will run most of the night. A cheap brushed motor on speed three will not reach 2am. Ask for the motor type and the current draw, not just the mAh.

The moment this matters

Eleven at night, the light goes, and the room is already warm. The children are asleep. You switch the fan to the speed that actually moves air, and you go to bed hoping. At two in the morning somebody is awake and crying because the fan stopped an hour ago. You bought a fan advertised at 20,000mAh. It should have lasted. It did not.

Runtime is a division, and most people are only told the top half

The arithmetic is simple and nobody prints it on the box:

Hours = battery capacity divided by current draw.

The box gives you the capacity. It almost never gives you the draw. So you are handed the numerator and asked to guess the denominator, and the denominator is where all the variation lives.

A 16 inch rechargeable fan with a cheap brushed motor typically pulls around 20 to 26 watts on its top speed. The same size fan with a brushless DC motor pulls roughly 8 to 12 watts for a similar amount of air. Same battery, and one of them empties it in less than half the time.

What we measured

In July 2026 we ran two 16 inch rechargeable fans of the same claimed 20,000mAh capacity from full charge until they stopped, in a room at normal Accra night temperature.

FanSpeed 1Speed 3
Brushed motorabout 7 hoursabout 3 hours 20 minutes
Brushless DC motorabout 14 hoursabout 6 hours 30 minutes

The brushless fan on speed one covered a full night with hours to spare. The brushed fan on speed three did not reach 2am, which is exactly the failure people describe.

Three things that decide your real hours

  • Motor type. Brushless DC is the single biggest factor. It is usually stated as "BLDC" or "DC motor" and it is worth paying for.
  • The speed you actually use. Dropping from speed three to speed one roughly doubles your night. Most rooms only need speed one once the air is moving.
  • Whether the light is on. The built-in LED panel on many of these fans is not free. Running it all night can cost you an hour or more.

The honest limitation

A rechargeable fan is a fan, not an inverter. It will not run a fridge, and it will not run all night on top speed no matter what the box says. If you need a whole room cooled through a long outage, you are looking at a different class of product and a different budget. We would rather tell you that now than sell you a disappointment.

What to ask before you buy

Ask three questions and you cannot go far wrong: is the motor brushless, what is the runtime on speed one, and does that figure include the light. If a seller cannot answer, they have not measured it.

Check it before you pay

At your door, before money: check the fan arrives charged enough to switch on, run it on each speed, and listen. A brushless motor is noticeably quieter and steadier. If it rattles or the speeds barely differ, do not pay.

See the rechargeable fans we stock, each listed with its motor type and the runtime we measured, not the runtime on the box. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: How To Check An Appliance At Your Door Before You Pay
excerpt: The rider is standing there. You have maybe two minutes. Here is exactly what to look at, in order, so you never pay for the wrong thing.
content:
Quick answer. You have about two minutes at the door and four checks that matter: the box seal, the plug and cable, the item against what you were told, and a five second power test. Do them in that order. If any one fails, do not pay. Pay on delivery only protects you if you actually use it.

The moment this matters

The rider calls from the gate. You come out, he hands you a box, and there is a small social pressure to just pay and go back inside. That pressure is exactly what a careless seller relies on. Two minutes of checking is the difference between a good purchase and a thing you regret for two years.

The four checks, in order

1. The box and the seal, ten seconds

Look for a factory seal, not tape that has been reapplied. Look for crushing at the corners. A resealed box does not automatically mean a bad item, but it means you check the contents harder before deciding.

2. The plug and cable, twenty seconds

This one is Ghana specific and it catches a lot of people. Your wall socket is Type G, the rectangular three pin. Anything arriving with a two pin European plug was built for a different market and will need an adapter, which is a fire risk on a heat appliance drawing real current.

Then run the cable through your fingers from plug to body. You are feeling for a joint, a lump of tape, or a section that feels thinner. A repaired cable on a new item means it is not new.

3. The item against what you were told, forty seconds

Take out your phone and read back the message. Model, size, capacity, colour, what was included. Check each one against the thing in your hands. A 1.8L kettle is not a 2L kettle. A blender that was described with a dry mill should have the dry mill cup in the box.

This is why we put the exact specification in the WhatsApp message rather than a vague product name. It gives you something to check against.

4. The five second power test, thirty seconds

Plug it in and switch it on. Do not run a kettle dry or a blender loaded, just prove it powers up and the motor or element responds.

  • Motors should start smoothly and settle to a steady note. A rattle or a note that wanders means a bearing or an unbalanced fan.
  • Heating elements should draw immediately. On a kettle you hear the water note begin within a few seconds.
  • Batteries should show a charge indicator. A rechargeable fan or lamp that arrives completely flat cannot be tested, so treat that as a reason to wait.

The four sentences that make this easy

Most people find the checking socially awkward rather than difficult. So use plain words and stay friendly. "Let me just open it small." "Let me check the plug." "Let me put it on for a second." "This one is not what we agreed, so I will not take it today."

A rider carrying a genuine item has no problem with any of that. Reluctance is itself information.

What we do differently, and why

We send the full specification in the order message on purpose, so you have a written thing to check against at the door. We deliver before we take money, so the risk sits with us and not with you. And if the item is not what we said, you do not pay and the rider takes it back. No argument, no deposit lost.

That policy costs us money on the rare occasions it happens. It is worth it, because the alternative is a market where nobody trusts anybody and everybody pays a little more to cover the risk.

One thing to avoid

Do not pay in advance for a discount. A price that is only available if you send money first is not a discount. It is the whole risk moving from the seller to you, priced at a few cedis.

See exactly how ordering works with us, or browse what we stock. You check it, then you pay the rider. Never the other way round.

title: Why Some Electric Kettles Rust Within A Year And Others Never Do
excerpt: Two kettles both say stainless steel. One is spotted with rust by the following harmattan. The difference is a number nobody prints on the box.
content:
Quick answer. "Stainless steel" is a family, not a grade. Kettles built with 201 grade steel corrode in a year or two in a humid kitchen. Kettles built with 304 grade last many years. The grade is rarely printed, so you judge it by the magnet test, the weld line and the weight.

The moment this matters

You reach for the kettle one morning and there is a rust bloom around the base of the element, or a brown speckle inside the spout. The kettle is fifteen months old. You did nothing wrong. You simply bought a grade of steel that was never going to survive a Ghanaian kitchen.

What the grades actually mean

Stainless steel resists rust because of chromium, and it resists it much better with nickel added. The two grades you meet on kettles:

GradeNickelBehaviour in a humid kitchen
201about 1%Cheaper. Corrodes at welds and around the element within one to two years.
304about 8%Standard for food equipment. Resists pitting for many years.

Nickel is the expensive ingredient, which is exactly why the cheaper kettle uses less of it. The saving is real and so is the consequence.

Three ways to tell them apart on the spot

  • The magnet test. 304 is essentially non-magnetic, so a fridge magnet slides off or clings very weakly. 201 has enough magnetic response that a magnet holds noticeably. This is not a laboratory test and cold working can affect it, but as a quick check at the door it is genuinely useful.
  • The weld line inside. Look down into the body at the vertical seam. A clean, even, barely visible weld suggests better manufacturing throughout. A rough, discoloured or pitted seam is where rust will start.
  • Weight. Pick up two kettles of the same capacity. The heavier one usually has thicker steel, which resists both corrosion and denting.

Why the water tastes different

The other thing people notice and rarely explain: a metallic taste in the first cup. That is usually not the steel body at all, it is an exposed heating element, the coil you can see sitting in the water. Exposed elements scale up quickly in hard water and shed that scale into your tea.

A concealed element, where the base is a flat plate and you see no coil, keeps the metal out of the water, descales far more easily, and is the single feature most worth paying a little more for.

What this costs in Accra

In July 2026 the working range we found across Accra dealers for a 1.8L to 2L kettle:

  • Plastic body, exposed element: GHS 90 to 120
  • 201 grade steel, exposed element: GHS 110 to 150
  • 304 grade steel, concealed element: GHS 160 to 230

The gap between the cheapest and the best here is roughly GHS 100. Spread over the extra years you get, it is the easiest upgrade decision in the whole kitchen.

Keeping it alive either way

Whatever grade you own, empty it after use rather than leaving water standing, and descale it monthly with vinegar or lime. Standing water plus an exposed element is how a kettle dies early.

Check it before you pay

At the door: look inside for a concealed flat base rather than a visible coil, run the magnet over the body, check the seam, and switch it on for five seconds to hear the element engage. If the body is magnetic and the element is exposed and you were told it was 304 with a concealed base, do not pay.

See the kettles we stock, with the element type stated on every one. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: Dry Iron Or Steam Iron For Kente, Lace And Everyday Clothes
excerpt: Steam is not automatically better. On kente, lace and most synthetics it is the thing that ruins them. Here is which iron suits which cloth.
content:
Quick answer. Steam relaxes fibres by wetting them, which is exactly right for cotton and linen and exactly wrong for kente, lace and most synthetics. For a Ghanaian wardrobe that mixes traditional cloth with office shirts, a dry iron plus a damp pressing cloth is the safer tool. Buy steam only if you press cotton shirts daily.

The moment this matters

You have a function on Saturday. The cloth has been folded for months and it needs pressing. You reach for the steam iron because steam sounds gentler, and you leave a shine on the fabric that will not come out. That mark is heat plus moisture plus pressure on threads that cannot take all three at once.

What steam actually does

Steam does not clean or protect. It wets the fibre so it becomes temporarily flexible, then the plate flattens it and it dries in the new shape. On cotton and linen, which are strong when wet, that is ideal and it is why a steam iron makes a shirt collar crisp in one pass.

On other fibres the same mechanism causes harm:

  • Kente and woven traditional cloth. The threads are tightly interlaced and often contain rayon or silk-like yarns. Wet heat plus pressure flattens the weave's texture and leaves a permanent sheen.
  • Lace. The open structure means the plate presses directly on individual threads with no cloth to spread the load. Steam softens them first, so they crush.
  • Polyester and most synthetics. These do not absorb water, they melt. Steam adds no benefit and the temperature needed to make steam is often above what the fibre tolerates.

The temperatures that matter

Irons hide this behind dots on a dial, which is why so many garments get damaged. In plain numbers:

SettingRoughlySafe for
One dot110 CNylon, acetate, most synthetics
Two dots150 CPolyester, silk, wool blends
Three dots200 CCotton, linen

Polyester begins to soften around 160 C. A three dot setting is comfortably past that, which is how a shirt gets a shiny patch in one careless pass.

The technique that protects traditional cloth

Use a dry iron on two dots, and put a thin cotton cloth between the plate and the garment. Dampen that pressing cloth, not the garment. You get controlled moisture spread evenly, the plate never touches the fibres directly, and the weave keeps its texture. This is how tailors do it and it costs nothing.

Which to buy

Dry iron if your wardrobe is mixed, if you own kente or lace, if you share the iron with people who will not check the dial, or if you want the simplest thing that lasts. Fewer parts, no water tank to scale up, and in a hard water area that matters.

Steam iron if you press cotton shirts most days and want speed. Buy one with a removable tank and descale it, because scale is what kills them.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026, across Accra dealers: a 1200W dry iron with a non-stick sole plate ran GHS 150 to 200. A comparable steam iron ran GHS 220 to 320. The dry iron is both cheaper and, for most Ghanaian wardrobes, the more suitable tool. That is not a compromise, it is a better match.

Check it before you pay

At the door: run a finger over the sole plate feeling for roughness or a nick, which will snag cloth. Switch it on and let it warm for thirty seconds to confirm the element and thermostat respond. Check the cable where it meets the body for a joint or tape.

See the irons we stock, with the sole plate type and wattage stated. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: Why Barbers Replace Blades, Not Clippers
excerpt: A clipper that pulls hair is almost never a dead motor. It is a dulled or misaligned blade, and that is a cheap fix most owners never make.
content:
Quick answer. The blade does the cutting and the motor only turns it, so blades wear out long before motors do. A clipper that pulls hair usually needs a blade replaced or realigned, not throwing away. Working barbers change blades every few months and keep the same clipper for years, which is why they buy for motor quality and blade availability, not for the accessory count in the box.

The moment this matters

You are halfway through a cut and the clipper starts pulling instead of cutting. The client winces. You push harder, which makes it worse. Most people conclude the clipper has died and buy another one. It has not died. Two cutting edges have gone slightly blunt, or drifted out of alignment by a fraction of a millimetre.

How a clipper actually cuts

A clipper is a pair of scissors repeated forty or so times across a comb, operating a few thousand times a minute. There is a fixed lower blade and a moving upper blade. Hair enters between the teeth and is sheared where the two edges cross.

Two things stop that shear working:

  • Dullness. The edges round over with use. A rounded edge folds hair instead of cutting it, and folded hair is what you feel as a pull.
  • Alignment. The moving blade should sit slightly back from the fixed blade, commonly a fraction under half a millimetre. Too far forward and it catches skin. Too far back and hair is not gripped at all. Dropping a clipper is the usual cause.

Neither of those is a motor problem, which is why replacing the whole machine is usually the expensive way to solve a cheap fault.

What a working barber does

Ask around any shop in Accra and the routine is consistent: oil the blade at the start and end of every day, brush the hair out of the teeth after each client, and replace the blade set when cutting starts to drag rather than waiting for it to fail. On a busy chair that is every few months. The clipper body itself lasts years.

It follows that the two things worth paying for are a motor that holds its speed under load, and a blade that is easy to buy again locally. A clipper with a superb motor and a blade nobody stocks in Ghana is a clipper with an expiry date.

The three motor types

MotorCharacterBest for
MagneticCheapest, noisy, loses speed in thick hairOccasional home use
PivotSlower blade, much more cutting forceThick and coarse hair, wet cutting
RotarySteady speed under load, quieter, usually cordlessProfessional all-day use

For dense African hair, force matters more than blade speed, which is why pivot and rotary machines dominate professional shops and magnetic ones mostly sit in bathrooms.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers: a rechargeable metal-body clipper suitable for daily home use ran GHS 95 to 180. Professional rotary machines ran GHS 350 upward. A replacement blade set for a common model ran GHS 35 to 60, which is the number most owners never learn and the reason so many working clippers get discarded.

Making yours last

  • Oil the blade before and after every session. Two drops across the teeth, run it for ten seconds, wipe the excess.
  • Brush hair out of the teeth. Trapped hair holds moisture and moisture rusts the edges.
  • Do not run a cordless clipper flat every time. Lithium cells last longer topped up than emptied.
  • If it starts pulling, replace the blade before you replace the clipper.

Check it before you pay

At the door: run it and listen for a steady note rather than a rattle. Look along the blade edge to confirm the moving blade sits slightly behind the fixed one and the teeth line up. Confirm the charging cable and any guards described are actually in the box.

title: Your First Place In Accra: The Seven Things You Actually Need
excerpt: Moving into your own place, the temptation is to buy everything at once. Here is the honest short list, what each costs now, and what can wait.
content:
Quick answer. Seven items cover cooking, light, cooling and laundry for a first place in Accra, and in July 2026 they came to roughly GHS 1,150 to 1,500 across Accra dealers. Everything else can wait a month without you suffering. Buy the light and the fan first, because an outage on your first night is a miserable introduction to independence.

The moment this matters

You have the keys. The room echoes. You have some money but not unlimited money, and everybody is telling you a different thing to buy first. The mistake almost everyone makes is buying decorative before functional, then discovering on night two that there is no light and nothing to boil water in.

The seven, in the order to buy them

1. Rechargeable lamp or emergency light, GHS 80 to 150

First, before anything. An outage on your first night in an unfamiliar room is genuinely unpleasant, and a phone torch drains the phone you need. Look for one that also charges a phone.

2. Rechargeable fan, GHS 250 to 420

Second. Sleep matters more than everything below this line. Buy brushless if you can stretch to it, because it roughly doubles the hours you get from the same battery.

3. Electric kettle, GHS 110 to 230

The most-used appliance in most first homes. Tea, koko, gari, washing water, and hot water for cooking faster. A concealed element costs a little more and descales far more easily.

4. Hot plate or table top cooker, GHS 180 to 380

Single burner for one person, double if you will actually cook two things at once. This is the item people over-buy. A single burner and a little patience covers a first year comfortably.

5. Blender, GHS 280 to 340

Only if you cook properly rather than reheating. Get the commercial-style one with a dry mill if you grind pepper. If you eat out most nights, this can wait a month.

6. Pressing iron, GHS 150 to 200

You need to look presentable for work. A dry iron is cheaper, simpler, and safer across a mixed wardrobe.

7. Drying rack, GHS 150 to 200

Underrated. If you are in a flat with no yard, this is the difference between clean clothes and damp clothes that smell.

The total, honestly

Cheapest sensible version of all seven: about GHS 1,150. Better version, with a brushless fan and a 304 steel kettle: about GHS 1,500. The extra GHS 350 mostly buys years rather than features, and the two places it matters most are the fan motor and the kettle steel.

What can wait

Microwave, air fryer, standing fan, speaker, cookware sets. All pleasant, none urgent. A microwave in particular is a month-two purchase for most people, because a hot plate does everything it does with a little more time.

Two mistakes worth avoiding

Buying the biggest number. The blender claiming 8000W is not more powerful than the one claiming 600W. A Ghanaian socket cannot deliver either figure, and the number on the box is a peak marketing claim rather than what the motor draws.

Paying before delivery. On a first move you are spending most of what you have. Do not send money to anyone before you have the item in your hands and have checked it. Nobody honest requires it.

How to do this in one order

title: What Each Appliance Costs To Run Per Month On The July 2026 Tariff
excerpt: PURC raised electricity 3.49% on 1 July 2026. Here is what that actually means per appliance, per month, in cedis, with the arithmetic shown.
content:
Quick answer. On the residential tariff effective 1 July 2026, standard households pay roughly GHS 2.04 per kWh below 300 units. At that rate a blender costs about GHS 6 a month, a kettle about GHS 25, a double hot plate about GHS 92, and a microwave about GHS 20. The appliances people fear are cheap. The ones that make heat are expensive.

The rate this is built on

The Public Utilities Regulatory Commission approved a 3.49% electricity increase effective 1 July 2026. For residential customers that puts the lifeline band at 89.93 pesewas per kWh, and standard residential consumption between roughly GHS 2.00 and GHS 2.65 per kWh depending on whether you are above or below 300 units in the month.

The figures below use GHS 2.04 per kWh, the standard residential rate below 300 units. If your household regularly passes 300 units, multiply everything here by about 1.3.

The arithmetic, so you can redo it

Monthly cost = watts ÷ 1000 × hours per day × 30 × tariff

Everything below is that one line, applied to realistic Ghanaian usage. Nothing here is a manufacturer figure.

The table

ApplianceReal drawTypical usekWh/monthCost/month
Blender600W10 min/day3.0GHS 6.11
Phone charging15W3 h/day1.4GHS 2.75
Rechargeable fan charging25W6 h/day4.5GHS 9.18
Microwave1200W18 min/day10.8GHS 22.03
Electric kettle2000W12 min/day12.0GHS 24.48
Pressing iron1200W30 min, 3x/week7.7GHS 15.71
Rice cooker700W40 min/day14.0GHS 28.56
Hot plate, single1500W1 h/day45.0GHS 91.80
Air fryer1400W25 min/day17.5GHS 35.70

The pattern nobody points out

Look down the list and one thing separates cheap from expensive, and it is not the size of the machine or the noise it makes. It is whether the appliance makes heat.

A blender has a motor and costs six cedis a month. A kettle has a heating element and costs four times that in a fraction of the running time. A hot plate is nothing but a heating element and it costs more than everything else on this list combined.

This matters because people worry about the wrong things. The blender with the frightening 8000W claim on the box is one of the cheapest things in your kitchen to run. The quiet little hot plate is the expensive one.

Three ways to actually cut the bill

  • Boil only what you need. A kettle costs the same per minute whether it holds one cup or two litres. Filling it out of habit is the most common avoidable cost in a Ghanaian kitchen.
  • Use the rice cooker instead of the hot plate where you can. It draws less than half and switches itself off.
  • Watch the 300 unit line. Crossing it moves your whole consumption to a higher band. If you are close, shifting one heat-heavy habit can keep you under it.

Honest limits of this page

These are calculations from measured draw and typical use, not meter readings from your house. Your actual bill depends on your habits, your tariff band, and the service charge. The method is exact; the inputs are averages. Redo the arithmetic with your own hours and you will get your own number.

title: Electric Hot Plate Or Gas: Which Is Actually Cheaper In Ghana
excerpt: Everyone assumes gas wins. The honest answer depends on two numbers, and one of them is efficiency, which nobody mentions. Here is the method.
content:
Quick answer. Gas holds more energy per cedi, but a gas hob wastes most of it heating the air around the pot. An electric hot plate converts a far higher share into the food. Once you correct for that, the two are much closer than people assume, and which wins depends on your current refill price. The method below lets you settle it for your own kitchen in two minutes.

Why the usual comparison is wrong

People compare the price of a kilogram of gas against the price of a unit of electricity. That comparison is meaningless, because it measures energy bought rather than energy delivered into the food.

A gas flame heats the pot and also heats the kitchen, your hand and the ceiling. A hot plate sits under the pot in direct contact. The share that actually reaches the food is very different:

Typical useful share
Gas hobabout 40%
Electric hot plateabout 70%

So gas has to be substantially cheaper per unit of energy just to draw level.

The method, in three lines

1. Electricity per useful kWh = tariff ÷ 0.70
At the July 2026 residential rate of GHS 2.04, that is GHS 2.91 per useful kWh.

2. Gas per useful kWh = (refill price per kg ÷ 13.8) ÷ 0.40
LPG holds roughly 13.8 kWh of energy per kilogram.

3. Compare the two. Whichever is lower wins for your kitchen this month.

Worked example

Say a refill works out at GHS 18 per kilogram.

Energy bought: 18 ÷ 13.8 = GHS 1.30 per kWh.
Energy delivered: 1.30 ÷ 0.40 = GHS 3.26 per useful kWh.

Against electricity at GHS 2.91, electricity is slightly cheaper at that refill price. At GHS 14 per kilogram, gas comes to GHS 2.54 and gas wins. The crossover in July 2026 sits around GHS 16 per kilogram. Check your own refill price and you will know immediately which side of the line you are on.

LPG prices move, sometimes weekly. That is exactly why we give you the method rather than a verdict that expires.

The things cost does not capture

Gas keeps working when the light goes. That is worth real money in a country with outages, and no arithmetic above accounts for it.

Electric is safer in a single room. No cylinder, no leak, no flame near a curtain. For a hostel or a rented single room this often decides it regardless of cost.

Gas has an entry cost. An empty 12.5kg cylinder runs several hundred cedis before you have bought any gas. A single burner hot plate is GHS 180 to 260 in Accra in July 2026 and needs nothing else.

Electric is slower. A hot plate takes noticeably longer to bring a big pot up. If you cook for a large household daily, that time is a real cost too.

Who should choose what

Hot plate if you are in a single room or hostel, cook for one or two, want the lowest entry cost, or cannot store a cylinder safely.

Gas if you cook large pots daily, you have somewhere safe outside the room for the cylinder, and you want cooking to be unaffected by outages.

Both is the honest answer for many households: gas for the big pot, hot plate for tea, small warming and the days you cannot get a refill.

One safety point that is not optional

A double burner hot plate can draw around 2,000W. A Ghanaian 13A socket tops out near 2,990W. Do not run a double hot plate and a kettle from the same extension board. That is how boards melt.

title: Why Rice Burns At The Bottom In Some Cookers And Crusts Perfectly In Others
excerpt: The same rice, the same water, two cookers, two completely different results. The difference is the pot, and it is visible before you buy.
content:
Quick answer. A rice cooker switches off when the pot passes 100 degrees, which happens when the free water is gone. What decides whether you get burnt rice or a good crust is how evenly the pot spreads heat in the seconds before that switch trips. A thick pot spreads it. A thin stamped pot creates a hot ring directly over the element and scorches there.

The moment this matters

You put on jollof, walk away, and come back to a black ring welded to the bottom of the pot and the smell through the whole house. The rice above it is fine. That pattern, burnt in a ring rather than burnt all over, tells you exactly what went wrong.

How a rice cooker knows to stop

There is no timer and no intelligence. Under the pot sits a spring-loaded magnetic thermostat. While free water remains, the pot cannot go above 100 degrees, because boiling water holds it there. The moment the last free water is absorbed or evaporated, the temperature climbs fast, the magnet loses its hold at around 103 degrees, and the switch clicks to warm.

That is the whole mechanism. It is elegant, it is cheap, and it means the cooker is blind to everything except the temperature at one point under the middle of the pot.

Where the burning comes from

The element is a ring, not the whole base. In the seconds between the last water going and the switch tripping, that ring is the hottest part of the pot.

  • A thick pot, or one with an aluminium layer bonded into the base, moves that heat sideways fast enough that no single spot gets far ahead. You get an even golden crust, which many people want.
  • A thin stamped pot cannot move heat sideways quickly. The ring over the element runs far hotter than the rest, and that is where the black circle forms.

So it is not the brand, the wattage, or the price. It is the thermal mass of the pot.

What to check before buying

  • Lift the inner pot out and feel the weight. This is the single best test and it takes two seconds. Heavier is better, every time.
  • Look at the base thickness at the rim where you can see the cross section. You want visible thickness, not foil.
  • Press the centre of the base gently. If it flexes, it is thin and it will scorch.
  • Check the non-stick coating is smooth and unbroken. A scratched coating is where sticking begins, and sticking becomes burning.

Cooking around a thin pot

If you already own one, three habits help. Add a spoon of oil to the water so the base layer is not dry rice against hot metal. Stir once when it comes to the boil so grains are not packed against the bottom. And open it as soon as it clicks to warm rather than leaving it sitting on the element.

On the crust, since people ask

A deliberate crust is not a fault. Plenty of people want it. The distinction is that a good crust is even, golden and lifts out in one piece, while a burn is a black ring welded in place. Even pots give you the first. Thin pots give you the second and no amount of technique fully fixes it.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers, a 1.8L rice cooker ran GHS 180 to 300. The difference between the ends of that range is almost entirely pot thickness and whether a real steamer basket is included. On this product, spending the extra buys you the thing that actually determines whether you like it.

Check it before you pay

At the door: take the inner pot out, feel the weight, press the centre, and look for scratches in the coating. Confirm the steamer basket is there if you were told it would be. Plug it in and confirm the switch clicks between cook and warm.

title: Solo Or Grill Microwave: What It Changes For Ghanaian Food
excerpt: A grill microwave costs more and most people never use the grill. Here is what each one actually does to food you cook here.
content:
Quick answer. A solo microwave heats by exciting water inside the food, which reheats rice and stew perfectly and cannot brown anything. A grill microwave adds a heating element on top that browns the surface. For Ghanaian cooking, which is mostly reheating rice, stew, banku and soup, the grill is rarely used. Buy solo unless you specifically want to brown chicken or melt cheese.

What a microwave actually does

Microwaves push water molecules in the food to vibrate, and that vibration is heat. The energy is generated inside the food rather than applied to the outside, which is why a plate of rice heats through in ninety seconds while an oven would take twenty minutes.

It also explains the limitation. Water cannot exceed 100 degrees while it is still water, and browning needs surface temperatures well above that. So a microwave physically cannot brown, crisp or roast. That is not a cheap microwave failing. That is the mechanism.

What the grill adds, and what it costs

A grill model puts a conventional heating element in the roof of the cavity. It browns from the outside like a normal grill, and it can be combined with the microwave function to heat through and brown at once.

Two honest caveats. The grill element makes the cavity genuinely hot, so a grill microwave is slower to cool and less pleasant in a small kitchen. And it draws real power, which changes the running cost from microwave-cheap to hot-plate-expensive for as long as it runs.

Which suits what you actually cook

DishSoloGrill adds
Reheating jollof or plain ricePerfectNothing
Reheating stew, soup, light soupPerfectNothing
Softening banku or kenkeyGood, cover itNothing
Reheating fried rice or chipsGoes softRestores some crispness
Browning chickenCannotYes, this is the case for it
Melting cheese on topMelts unevenlyYes
Defrosting meat and fishGood on low powerNothing

Read that column honestly. For most Ghanaian households, the grill earns its keep on two rows out of seven.

The size question

20 litres is the common size and it suits one to four people. It takes a standard dinner plate but not a large casserole dish. If you regularly reheat a full family pot, measure your biggest dish before you buy, because the frustration of a dish that does not fit never goes away.

What it costs to run

A 20L microwave draws around 1200W while running. At the July 2026 residential tariff of GHS 2.04 per kWh, eighteen minutes a day works out at roughly GHS 22 a month. That is cheap for the amount of reheating it does, and far cheaper than doing the same reheating on a hot plate, which would cost several times more for the same job because it heats the pot, the air and the room.

Two things that shorten a microwave's life

  • Running it empty. With no water to absorb the energy, it reflects back into the magnetron. A few seconds is survivable, a few minutes is not.
  • Metal. Not just foil. The metal rim on a decorated plate will arc. If in doubt, plain ceramic or glass.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers: a 20L solo microwave ran GHS 850 to 1,100, and comparable grill models sat above that range. If you will use the grill twice a year, that difference buys a rice cooker instead.

Check it before you pay

At the door: open and close the door and feel the latch engage firmly, because the safety interlock is the one part that must not be loose. Put a cup of water in and run it for thirty seconds to confirm it heats. Check the turntable and its roller ring are both in the box.

title: School Bags That Survive A Full Ghanaian School Year
excerpt: Most school bags fail in the same three places, always before Christmas. Here is what to check in the shop, and what a set should cost before term opens.
content:
Quick answer. School bags fail at the zip, the shoulder strap join, and the bottom seam, almost always in that order. Check those three points and a GHS 250 set outlasts three GHS 120 bags. Buy before the last week of the holiday, when stock is picked over and prices firm up.

The moment this matters

It is the second week of November. The zip has separated, the bag is being carried under one arm, books are getting rained on, and you are buying a second bag for the same child in the same term. The first bag did not wear out. It failed at one of three specific points, and all three were visible in the shop.

The three failure points, in order

1. The zip

This is the first thing to go on almost every cheap bag. What matters is the size of the teeth and the material. Look for a moulded plastic zip in size 5 or larger, or a metal zip. A thin coil zip on a bag that will be stuffed past its capacity every day will separate within a term.

Test it in the shop: run it fully closed and then press the two sides apart with your thumbs. A good zip resists. A weak one starts to gape and that gape becomes a split.

2. Where the shoulder strap meets the body

This is where the whole weight of the books actually lives. You want to see a box stitch, a square of stitching with a cross through it, or at minimum a bar tack, the dense block of thread. A single line of stitching there will pull out.

Turn the bag inside out if you can. Good bags have webbing that continues into the body rather than being sewn onto the surface.

3. The bottom seam and corners

Bags get dropped, dragged and put down on wet ground. A reinforced or double-layered base, ideally with a separate panel, survives that. A single layer of the same fabric as the sides will fray at the corners first and then split.

Fabric, honestly

Most school bags are polyester, quoted as 600D or 900D. The D is denier, the thread thickness. Higher is tougher. 600D is adequate for a light load, 900D or above is what you want for a secondary school student carrying real weight.

Water resistance matters here more than in many markets, because of how the rainy season and the school run interact. A coated inner face and a flap that covers the zip line are worth more than any branding.

Fit, which affects the child more than the bag

  • The bag should sit between the shoulders and the waist, not hang below the hips.
  • Both straps, always. A heavy bag on one shoulder puts real strain on a growing spine.
  • A padded back panel is not luxury if the child walks any distance, because book corners press through thin fabric.
  • A chest clip, if it has one, keeps the straps from sliding off the shoulders and is genuinely useful for younger children.

What a set costs, July 2026

Across Accra dealers this month, a five in one school backpack set, the bag with a lunch bag, pencil case and small accessories, ran GHS 220 to 280. A standalone bag of similar build quality ran GHS 120 to 190.

The set is usually better value if the child needs the lunch bag anyway, which most do.

Timing

Buy in the first half of the holiday. In the last week before term opens, the good sizes and the stronger builds are gone, and what remains is whatever nobody chose. That is the single easiest saving available on this purchase.

Check it before you pay

At the door: work the zip fully both ways and press it apart. Pull firmly on each shoulder strap where it joins the body. Look at the base corners for a second layer. Confirm everything in the set is actually in the bag.

title: How To Spot A Fake Power Bank Capacity Before You Buy
excerpt: A power bank that weighs 180 grams cannot hold 30,000mAh. Physics will not allow it. Here are four checks you can do standing at the door.
content:
Quick answer. Lithium cells have a known energy density, so a real 20,000mAh power bank cannot weigh less than roughly 300 grams. If it is light, the capacity is invented. Weight, count of full phone charges, charge time and price are four checks that catch almost every exaggerated claim, and you can do all four before you pay.

Two different problems, often confused

There is honest loss and there is invented capacity, and they are not the same thing.

Honest loss is physics. Cells run at 3.7 volts, your phone charges at 5 volts, and converting between them loses energy as heat. A genuine 20,000mAh bank delivers roughly 12,000 to 13,000mAh into a phone. Every honest manufacturer has this loss. We have written about it separately.

Invented capacity is different. It is a bank containing cells totalling 6,000mAh with 30,000 printed on the case. No physics involved, just a number.

Check 1: weight, and it is the strongest

Lithium polymer cells hold a fairly narrow range of energy per gram. Working backwards from that, a genuine bank cannot be lighter than roughly:

Claimed capacityMinimum plausible weight
10,000mAhabout 180 g
20,000mAhabout 330 g
30,000mAhabout 480 g

A "30,000mAh" bank that feels like a phone in your hand is not a 30,000mAh bank. This single check catches most of them, needs no equipment, and cannot be argued with.

Check 2: count the charges

Take your own phone's battery, commonly 4,500 to 5,000mAh on a modern Android. A genuine 20,000mAh bank should give you between two and a half and three full charges. If a seller claims six, they are quoting the cell capacity without the conversion loss, which is either ignorance or a sales tactic.

Ask this question directly: how many full charges of a 5,000mAh phone? An honest seller says two and a half to three for a 20,000. Anyone who says five or six has told you something useful about themselves.

Check 3: charge time

Energy in and energy out follow the same arithmetic. A genuine 20,000mAh bank charged at a normal 2A takes many hours, commonly eight to twelve. If a bank claiming 30,000mAh reaches full in two hours on an ordinary charger, it did not store 30,000mAh, because it was never asked to.

Check 4: price sanity

Cells are the dominant cost. In July 2026 in Accra, an honest 10,000mAh bank ran GHS 110 to 160 and a genuine 20,000mAh ran GHS 150 to 260. A "30,000mAh" offered at GHS 90 has not found a clever supplier. It contains roughly GHS 90 worth of cells, which is not 30,000mAh.

What to look for on the case

A real specification lists both the cell capacity in mAh and the energy in watt-hours, something like 74Wh. Watt-hours are harder to fake convincingly because the arithmetic is checkable: watt-hours equals mAh times 3.7 divided by 1,000. If the two numbers on the case do not agree with each other, one of them is decoration.

Also check the output rating. A bank with a single 1A output will charge a modern phone slowly regardless of its capacity. 2A minimum, and look for USB-C with Power Delivery if you have a recent phone.

Check it before you pay

At the door: hold it and judge the weight against the table above, read the case for a watt-hour figure that agrees with the mAh, confirm the output is at least 2A, and plug your own phone in to see it start charging. If it feels light for its claim, do not pay.

title: Why One Earbud Always Dies Before The Other
excerpt: It is almost never a fault. There is a specific reason the same earbud goes flat first, and one habit that roughly doubles how long the pair lasts.
content:
Quick answer. In most wireless earbuds one bud is the master: it holds the connection to your phone and relays audio to the other. That extra radio work drains it faster, so it dies first, every time. Swapping which bud you use first does not help, because the role is usually fixed in firmware. Charging the pair before they are fully flat helps considerably.

The moment this matters

You are on a trotro, an hour into a journey, and the right bud cuts out. The left one keeps playing, which is somehow more annoying than both stopping. You assume you bought a faulty pair. You did not.

The master and slave arrangement

Your phone does not maintain two separate connections. It connects to one earbud, and that earbud forwards the audio to its partner over a second short-range link.

So one bud is doing two jobs: receiving from the phone and transmitting to the other bud. The other is only receiving. Radio transmission is the expensive part of the work, which is why the same side runs down first. On many models it is the right bud by convention, but it varies.

Newer premium designs use a scheme where both buds listen to the phone independently, and some alternate the master role between them. Those pairs drain evenly. Most budget earbuds sold here do not work that way.

Why swapping which one you put in first does nothing

People try this and conclude the earbuds are faulty when it fails. The master role is set in the firmware, not by which one you take out of the case first. Unless the specification explicitly mentions role switching, you cannot change it.

The habit that actually extends their life

This is the part worth knowing, because it affects how long the whole pair survives, not just one session.

Lithium cells age fastest when they are held at the extremes: fully charged for long periods, or run completely flat. Small earbud cells are especially sensitive because there is so little capacity to buffer the stress.

  • Put them back in the case when you finish rather than leaving them out until they die. The case tops them up gently.
  • Do not leave the case plugged in overnight, every night. Hours at 100% is exactly the condition that ages cells.
  • Do not store them flat for weeks. A cell left fully discharged can drop below the voltage at which it will accept charge again, and then it is finished.

The pair you charge sensibly can last two to three times as long as one that is run flat and left on the charger.

The battery hours question

Advertised playtime is measured at a low volume, usually around half. Most people listen louder than that, especially on a trotro or a busy street, and the amplifier draws far more at high volume. A pair advertised at six hours commonly gives around three at a usable volume in a noisy place. That is not the seller lying, it is the test condition being unrealistic for Ghana.

So when you compare two pairs, compare their advertised numbers against each other rather than treating either as what you will actually get.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers, wireless earbuds ran GHS 90 to 250. The useful difference across that range is real battery capacity, whether the case charges over USB-C, and whether the microphone is usable on a call. Very little of it is sound quality, which plateaus early in this category.

Check it before you pay

At the door: pair them with your own phone, play something with both in, and take a short call to hear whether the microphone is acceptable. Check both buds sit in the case and the case shows them charging. If one will not pair or seat properly, do not pay.

title: Why A Small Bluetooth Speaker Sounds Thin, And What To Look At Instead Of Watts
excerpt: The watt number on the box tells you almost nothing about how a speaker sounds. Two physical things do, and you can judge both by hand.
content:
Quick answer. Bass needs the speaker to move air, and the amount of air it can move is set by the size of the driver and the volume of the box behind it. A small speaker cannot move much air whatever wattage is printed on it. Judge by driver diameter, box size and whether it has a passive radiator. Ignore the watts.

Why the watt number misleads

Watts measure how much electrical power the amplifier can push, not how much sound comes out or what it sounds like. Two speakers rated the same can be completely different, and the ratings themselves are often peak figures rather than sustained ones.

Worse, on cheap units the number is frequently just marketing, the same way blender wattage is. A pocket speaker claiming 20W has not found a way around physics.

What actually makes bass

Low frequencies are long pressure waves. To create them you have to move a meaningful quantity of air. Two things decide how much air a speaker can move:

  • Driver diameter. A larger cone moves more air per stroke. This is why a 3 inch driver produces bass a 1.5 inch driver simply cannot, at any wattage.
  • Enclosure volume. The air trapped behind the cone acts like a spring. A tiny sealed box makes a stiff spring that resists the cone moving far, which cuts the low end. This is the real reason pocket speakers sound thin and no equaliser setting fixes it.

You can hear this any time you cup your hand behind a small speaker and the sound changes. You have altered the enclosure.

The passive radiator, which is worth understanding

Look at the ends of many cylindrical Bluetooth speakers and you will see what appears to be a second speaker with no wires, often a flat disc that visibly moves when bass plays. That is a passive radiator, an undriven cone tuned to resonate at low frequencies.

It lets a small box behave acoustically like a larger one, and it is the single most effective trick in portable speaker design. A speaker with visible passive radiators will almost always have more useful bass than a same-sized one without.

What to judge in the shop

Look atWhy
Driver diameterBigger cone, more air, more bass. The one number that reliably correlates with sound.
Overall box size and weightA heavier speaker of the same size usually has a real magnet and a braced box.
Passive radiatorsVisible discs at the ends that move with bass. A genuine design decision, not a sticker.
Battery capacity in mAhPlaytime claims are measured at low volume. The mAh figure is harder to inflate.
Watt ratingAlmost nothing. Ignore it.

Outdoors changes everything

Indoors, walls reflect sound back and reinforce the low end, so a small speaker sounds fuller than it is. Outside there is nothing to reflect, the bass disappears, and you discover what you actually bought.

If the speaker is for outdoor use, for a compound, a small gathering, or a beach, size is not negotiable. This is the one purchase where buying the physically bigger unit is almost always right.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers, portable Bluetooth speakers ran GHS 180 to 400. Within that range the difference that matters is driver size and whether there are passive radiators, not the wattage claim, and not the brand.

Check it before you pay

At the door: pair it with your own phone and play something you know well, with real bass, at about three quarters volume. Listen for the cone bottoming out, a rattling or farting sound, which means the driver is being pushed past what it can do. Check the charging port and confirm it holds a connection when you walk a few metres away.

title: 230V At 50Hz: What Ghana's Supply Means For Appliances Brought From Abroad
excerpt: An appliance bought in the US or Dubai may work here, may work badly, or may destroy itself in seconds. Which one depends on two numbers on the label.
content:
Quick answer. Ghana supplies 230 volts at 50 hertz through Type G and Type D sockets. An appliance labelled 100 to 240V will work here with only a plug adapter. An appliance labelled 110 to 120V will be destroyed, often instantly, unless you run it through a step-down transformer sized for its wattage. Read the label before you plug anything in.

The label is the whole answer

Every appliance carries a rating plate, usually on the base or the back near the cable. It gives an input voltage and a frequency. Those two figures decide everything.

Label saysIn GhanaWhat you need
100 to 240V, 50/60HzWorks normallyPlug adapter only
220 to 240V, 50HzWorks normallyPlug adapter if the pins differ
110 to 120V onlyWill be damagedStep-down transformer rated above the appliance wattage
Voltage fine, 60Hz onlyRuns, but slowerUsually acceptable; see below

The voltage part, plainly

Feeding a 120V appliance 230V does not make it work harder. It roughly quadruples the power dissipated in its components, because power rises with the square of voltage. Heating elements glow and fail. Motors burn their windings. Electronics let go immediately, often with a bang.

There is no gentle version of this mistake. A 120V kettle plugged into a Ghanaian socket is destroyed before you can unplug it.

The frequency part, which people ignore

Frequency matters less, but not never. A simple motor designed for 60Hz runs about 17% slower on our 50Hz supply. On a fan you would barely notice. On a washing machine, a food processor or anything with a timer driven by mains frequency, it means slower spinning and longer cycles than intended.

The bigger issue is heat. A 60Hz motor on 50Hz can run hotter because its magnetic circuit was designed around the higher frequency. It will usually work. It will usually not last as long.

Transformers, if you must

If you genuinely need to run a 120V appliance here, a step-down transformer is the only correct answer, and it must be rated comfortably above the appliance's wattage. A 500W transformer will not run a 1,200W hair dryer, and trying is a fire risk rather than a disappointment.

The honest advice: for anything with a heating element, do not bother. The transformer costs more than buying the correct appliance locally, and it sits there consuming power and getting hot for the life of the thing.

Our two socket types

Type G is the rectangular three pin, rated 13 amps, which at 230 volts is a ceiling of 2,990 watts. It has a fuse in the plug, which is a genuine safety feature.

Type D is the older round three pin, rated 6 amps, a ceiling of 1,380 watts. If you are still on Type D sockets, a 2,000W kettle is already past what that circuit was designed for.

This is also why every blender box claiming 4,500W or 8,000W is quoting a figure no Ghanaian socket can deliver.

Adapters versus converters

These get confused constantly and the difference matters. An adapter only changes the shape of the pins. It does nothing to the voltage. A converter or transformer changes the voltage. Putting a 120V appliance into a plug adapter gives it the full 230V and destroys it. If the label does not say 240V, an adapter alone is not enough.

Protecting what you already own

Voltage on our network is not perfectly steady, and the surge when power returns after an outage is when appliances most often die. A surge protector on anything with electronics inside, a microwave, a television, a decoder, costs far less than the thing it protects.

Everything we sell is specified for 230V, 50Hz and Type G, because it is bought for this market rather than imported for another one. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: Making A Blender Last: The Five Habits That Decide Whether It Survives Two Years
excerpt: Blenders here rarely die of old age. They die of five specific habits, and four of them cost nothing to change.
content:
Quick answer. Most blenders in Ghana fail from heat, from a stripped coupling, or from water reaching the motor, not from wearing out. Run in bursts rather than continuously, add a little liquid to hard grinding, never wash the base, replace the coupling instead of the machine, and stop when it smells hot. Those five habits are the difference between one year and five.

Why blenders die here specifically

A blender used for smoothies runs for thirty seconds against soft fruit. A blender used in a Ghanaian kitchen grinds dried pepper, ginger, garlic and groundnut, often dry, often in a full jar, sometimes for minutes at a time. That is a much harder duty, and the failures follow from it.

1. Run in bursts, not continuously

The motor is cooled by a small fan on its own shaft, and that cooling cannot keep up with a heavy grinding load. Heat is what kills the winding insulation, and once that goes the motor is finished.

Work in bursts of about thirty seconds with a pause between. It takes the same total time because the pauses let the load settle back onto the blade anyway, and the motor stays far cooler. If the base is too hot to rest your hand on, stop and let it cool completely.

2. Give hard grinding a little help

Dry pepper packed into a jar climbs the walls and spins around the blade in a pocket of air, so the motor works hard and nothing gets ground. A spoon of water or oil, or simply grinding in smaller batches, keeps material falling back onto the blade.

If your machine has a dry mill cup, use it for genuinely dry work. It is designed with the right jar geometry and it saves the main motor a great deal of strain.

3. Never put the base in water

Obvious, and still the second most common cause of death. The motor, the switch and the wiring are all in that base. Wipe it with a damp cloth and dry it.

The subtler version of this mistake: overfilling the jar so liquid runs down the outside and pools where the jar meets the base. Fill to the line, not to the brim.

4. Replace the coupling, not the blender

The coupling is the small toothed part joining motor to jar, and on a machine used daily it is a wear item. When it strips, the motor spins and the blade does not, and the machine sounds like it is running perfectly while doing nothing.

Most people conclude the blender is dead. It is not. A coupling is a cheap part and it is the single most common repair on these machines. This is also why a metal coupling is worth paying for at purchase.

5. Stop the moment it smells hot

That sharp, electrical smell is insulation beginning to break down. It is not a normal smell and it does not clear. Switch off, unplug, and let it cool for an hour. Continuing through it is how a recoverable overheat becomes a burnt-out motor.

The seal, while you are at it

The rubber gasket between the blade assembly and the jar hardens over time, and once it leaks you get liquid running into the coupling and eventually into the base. If you see moisture around the base of the jar after blending, replace the gasket. It costs very little and it prevents the expensive failure.

What running one actually costs

Ten minutes of blending a day on a 600W machine works out at about GHS 6 a month at the July 2026 residential tariff of GHS 2.04 per kWh. Electricity is not what a blender costs you. Replacing it every eighteen months is.

When it genuinely is finished

If the motor turns but has no force under load, if it trips your breaker, or if it sparks visibly through the base vents, that is the end. Anything else, particularly a machine that spins freely without turning the blade, is very likely a coupling.

See the blenders we stock, with the coupling material stated on each one, because it is the part that decides how long the machine lasts. Pay on delivery in Accra.
